dedupe_keys.name: piping botnet smart irrigation controllers as an attack vector against urban water services

description: The Piping Botnet study shows how internet-connected smart irrigation controllers, sold as green technology to save water, could be turned into a botnet that drains an urban water supply. The authors present an attack model and test it on three commercial controllers: a compromised device on the local network detects a controller within 15 minutes with a classifier, then starts watering by spoofing and replaying commands. Their damage model finds that 1,355 sprinklers could empty a standard water tower in an hour and 23,866 could empty a flood reservoir overnight. Coverage is the attack concept applied to urban water services in general. Format and access: an arXiv preprint under the arXiv distribution licence; free to read; no data or code is released. Caveats: the results come from lab tests of three products and a model, and vendors may have patched the flaws since 2018. It supports resilience studies of cyber threats to irrigation and water networks. A related catalogue record is the interdependent water and power infrastructure model.

name: Piping Botnet: smart irrigation controllers as an attack vector against urban water services
outcomes: A bot on a compromised LAN can identify a smart irrigation controller and launch watering; the damage model shows a standard water tower emptied in an hour with 1,355 sprinklers and a flood reservoir emptied overnight with 23,866 sprinklers. Countermeasures are discussed; no dataset is released.
